title: Small arguments evaluate x*N(t)/D(t) on the x87 unit with stored steps, and the last bit can be high
statement: For normal x with |x| < 2^-16, ERF.PRECISE computes x*N(t)/D(t) with t = x^2 on the x87 unit at precision 64: N and D are each stored to binary64, then the product, then the quotient. Below 2^-27 this reduces to p = RN53(RN64(x*P0)) and y = RN53(RN64(p/Q0)), with P0 = 0x3ff1df5e70c7956b and Q0 = 0x3fefada15778ece6. The coefficient table is unidentified: Cody's 1969 rational shares the constant-term ratio, as any accurate table does, but its normalised linear terms differ (0.1176 and 0.4510 against Excel's 0.1259 and 0.4593), and Cephes and fdlibm also miss. The rounded steps can leave the answer 1 unit above the correctly rounded erf(x), as the rows below show. The same route explains GAUSS's small arguments.
basis: All 499,814 recorded ERF.PRECISE rows with 0 < |x| < 2^-16 match; per-operation binary64 misses rows in the 2^-40 binade alone (131,201 of 131,255). Bisecting live Excel to one input ulp located where stored D and stored N first step, and every answer fit those two hypotheses. The measured coefficients give N1/N0 - D1/D0 = -1/3 to 1.2e-16, which is erf's Taylor coefficient and was not imposed by the measurement.
inferred: That the legacy ERF(x) shares this body is inferred; only ERF.PRECISE and GAUSS rows were scored. D1 is one of two adjacent values that no recorded answer separates.

correct.how: mpmath erf at 800 bits from the binary64 input, correctly rounded.
